The fierce one, bhikkhus, who is fierce by nature, fierce in character, fierce in temperament; the fierce one who is fierce in his speech; the fierce one who is fierce in both speech and action; and the fierce one who is fierce neither in speech nor in action, but who is fierce in his underlying tendency. Here, someone speaks harshly to his mother, his father, his brother, his sister, his friends, companions, kinsmen, and relatives; he speaks harshly to ascetics and brahmins. Then Caṇḍa the headman approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Caṇḍa the headman said this to the Blessed One:
“What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason why someone here comes to be known as ‘violent,’ precisely because of his violence?”
“But what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason why someone here is reckoned as ‘gentle’ only because of his gentleness?
“Here, headman, a certain person has not abandoned lust.
Because lust has not been abandoned, he provokes others; being provoked by others, he manifests anger.”
Thus he comes to be known as "the fierce one.
Hatred is not abandoned.
Because hatred is not abandoned, he provokes others; being provoked by others, he manifests anger.
Thus he comes to be known as "the fierce one.
Delusion has not been abandoned.
Because delusion has not been abandoned, he provokes others to anger; being provoked by others, he manifests anger himself.
And thus he comes to be known as "fierce.
This, headman, is the cause, this is the condition why someone here who is fierce comes to be known as "fierce.
But in this case, headman, someone has abandoned lust.
Because lust has been abandoned, he does not provoke others; even when provoked by others, he does not manifest anger.
He comes to be known as one who is gentle.
Hatred has been abandoned.
Because hatred has been abandoned, he does not provoke others; even when provoked by others, he does not manifest anger.
He comes to be known as one who is gentle.
Delusion has been abandoned.
“Because delusion has been abandoned, he does not provoke others; even when provoked by others, he does not manifest anger.
Thus, he comes to be known as ‘gentle.
This, headman, is the cause, this is the reason why someone here who is gentle comes to be known as ‘gentle.’”
When this was said, Caṇḍa the headman said to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Bhante! Excellent, Bhante!
Just as, Bhante, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost...”
Or one might show the way, or one might hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
just so has the Dhamma been proclaimed by the Blessed One in many ways.
Therefore, venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
Thus [he spoke]. First.

1. Gāmaṇivagga: The Discourse to Tālapuṭa.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.

Then Tālapuṭa, the chief of actors, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Tālapuṭa, the chief of actors, said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, I have heard this from the actors of old, the teachers of former teachers, as they were speaking:

'That actor who, in the midst of the stage, in the midst of the assembly, makes people laugh and delight by means of truth and falsehood, at the breaking up of the body, after death, is reborn in the company of the laughing devas.'"
“What does the Blessed One say about this?
“Enough, headman; let that be. Do not ask me that.
A second time, the headman Tālapuṭa said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I have heard this from the actors of old, the teachers of former teachers, as they were speaking:

‘That actor who, in the midst of the stage, in the midst of the assembly, makes people laugh and delight by means of truth and falsehood, upon the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in the company of the laughing devas.
What does the Blessed One say about this?”
“Enough, head of the village; let this be. Do not ask me this.
A third time, the actor-headman Tālapuṭa said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I have heard this from the actors of old, the teachers of teachers, as they were speaking:”

‘That actor who, in the midst of the stage and in the midst of the assembly, makes people laugh and delight with truth and falsehood, will, upon the breakup of the body after death, be reborn in the company of the Laughing Devas.
What does the Blessed One say about this?
“Certainly, headman, I do not grant you that.”
“Enough, headman; let this be.
Do not ask me this.
Nevertheless, I shall explain it to you.
Formerly, headman, beings were not free from lust and were bound by the bond of lust;
for them, the actor, in the midst of the stage and the midst of the assembly, presents those things that are provocative of lust to an even greater degree.
Formerly, headman, beings were not free from hatred and were bound by the bond of hatred.
In their midst, amidst the stage and the assembly, the actor presents those things that are provocative of hatred to an even greater degree.
Previously, headman, beings were not free from delusion and were bound by the fetter of delusion.
In their midst, amidst the stage and the assembly, the actor presents those things that are provocative of delusion to an even greater degree.
Thus, being intoxicated and heedless oneself, and having made others intoxicated and heedless, with the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn in the hell named Pahāsa (the Laughing Hell).
Furthermore, if one holds such a view as this:

“That actor who, in the midst of the stage or the arena, makes people laugh and delight them with truth and falsehood, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in companionship with the Pahāsa devas,” that is his wrong view.
“Furthermore, headman, for a person of wrong view, I declare one of two destinations:
either hell or the animal realm.
When this was said, Tālapuṭa, the headman of the actors, wept and shed tears.
“Indeed, headman, I did not get this from you:
‘Enough, headman, let this be; do not ask me this.
“I am not weeping, Bhante, because the Blessed One said this to me.”
"Moreover, venerable sir, for a long time I have been led astray, deceived, and deluded by actors of old, the teachers of my teachers, who said:

'That actor who, in the midst of the stage, in the midst of the assembly, makes people laugh and delight with truth and falsehood, upon the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in the company of the laughing devas.
"Excellent, venerable sir! Excellent, venerable sir!"
"Just as, venerable sir, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden,
or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
even so has the Dhamma been elucidated by the Blessed One in many ways."
“Venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May I receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One, venerable sir; may I receive full ordination.
Tālapuṭa, the chief actor, received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; he received full ordination.
And not long after his full ordination, the Venerable Tālapuṭa ... [as before] ...
became one of the Arahants.
This is the second [discourse].

Gāmaṇivagga Yodhājīvasutta – The Warrior “Monks, suppose a warrior were to say this: ‘I will not fight with anyone who does not have a sword and shield, who is not wearing armor, and who does not carry a bow and arrows. It is impossible that he would find anyone to fight with. Why is that? Because he has set such a condition for himself. In the same way, monks, it is impossible for a person who holds wrong view, who holds a distorted perspective, to enter the path of the noble ones, to enter the way of the noble ones, to enter the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Why is that? Because he has set such a condition for himself. But, monks, it is possible for a person who holds right view, who holds an undistorted perspective, to enter the path of the noble ones, to enter the way of the noble ones, to enter the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Why is that? Because he has not set such a condition for himself.”

For a third time, the village headman Yodhājīva said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I have heard this from the warriors of old, the teachers and preceptors of our forefathers, as they were speaking:

‘That warrior who exerts himself and strives in battle, if he is slain or killed by his enemies while thus exerting himself and striving, then with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of the Parajita devas.’”
"What does the Blessed One say about this?
"Certainly, headman, I cannot say to you:
'Enough, headman, let this be; do not ask me that.'"
Moreover, I shall explain this to you.
Village headman, when that warrior exerts himself and strives in battle, his mind is already seized by an evil and wrongly directed thought:
"May these beings be slain, or bound, or cut off, or destroyed, or may they not even exist!"
While he is striving and exerting himself, others kill him and finish him off;
with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the hell named Parājita.
But if he holds such a view as this:
‘If that warrior who exerts himself and strives in battle is slain or killed by his enemies while exerting himself and striving,
then with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in the company of the Parajita devas’—
this is his wrong view.
“Furthermore, headman, for a person of wrong view, I declare one of two destinations:
either hell or the animal realm.
When this was said, the headman Yodhājīva wept and shed tears.
“Gāmaṇi, it was for this reason that I did not grant you leave, saying:
‘Enough, Gāmaṇi! Let this be; do not ask me this.
“I am not weeping, Bhante, because the Blessed One said this to me.”
"Moreover, venerable sir, for a long time I have been deceived, cheated, and deluded by the warriors of old, my teachers' teachers, who said:

1. Gāmaṇivagga: Hatthārohasutta. Then the elephant trainer, the village headman, approached the Blessed One; having approached, ... [as before] ... he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the elephant trainer, the village headman, said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. "Headman, when a noble disciple possesses four things, he is one who has transcended the realm of Māra, transcended the realm of the passing of time, transcended the realm of Death, transcended all suffering; he is a person who has reached the ultimate end, a person who has accomplished the task, a person who has laid down the burden, a person who has lived the holy life, a person whose taints are destroyed, a person who has attained final knowledge, a person who is a supramundane victor, one who cannot be measured by the world. "Venerable sir, what are those four things? "Headman, here a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: 'The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: 'The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: 'The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—untorn, unrent, unblotched, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. Headman, when a noble disciple possesses these four things, he is one who has transcended the realm of Māra, transcended the realm of the passing of time, transcended the realm of Death, transcended all suffering; he is a person who has reached the ultimate end, a person who has accomplished the task, a person who has laid down the burden, a person who has lived the holy life, a person whose taints are destroyed, a person who has attained final knowledge, a person who is a supramundane victor, one who cannot be measured by the world. "Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. Thus spoke the elephant trainer, the village headman. The Teacher approved. Then the elephant trainer, the village headman, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Then, not long after the elephant trainer, the village headman, had left, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, even if a noble disciple were to possess only this much, namely, confirmed confidence in the Buddha, he would still be one who has transcended the realm of Māra, transcended the realm of the passing of time, transcended the realm of Death, transcended all suffering; he would be a person who has reached the ultimate end, a person who has accomplished the task, a person who has laid down the burden, a person who has lived the holy life, a person whose taints are destroyed, a person who has attained final knowledge, a person who is a supramundane victor, one who cannot be measured by the world. How much more so, monks, when he possesses all these four things! Thus spoke the Blessed One. 1. The Chapter on Village Headmen:

The Discourse on the Horseman Then the village headman Assāroha approached the Blessed One; having approached, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the village headman Assāroha said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I have heard this from the teachers of old, the preceptors of former times, as they were speaking to horsemen:

‘When a horseman exerts himself and strives in battle, if others kill him while he is exerting himself and striving, or cause him to perish, then with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of the gods who are victorious in battle.
What does the Blessed One say about this?”
“Enough, headman, let this be; do not ask me that.
A second time...
and a third time, the headman Assāroha said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I have heard this from the teachers of old, the preceptors of former times, who were horse-riders, as they spoke thus:

‘When a horse-rider exerts himself and strives in battle, if others kill him while he is exerting himself and striving, or cause him to perish, then with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of the Parajita devas.
What does the Blessed One say about this?”
“Certainly, headman, I cannot say to you:
‘Enough, headman, let this be; do not ask me this.
Nevertheless, I shall answer you.”
“Headman, when a horse-rider exerts himself and strives in battle, his mind has previously been seized by what is wrong and ill-directed:
‘May these beings be slain, or bound, or cut off, or destroyed, or may they cease to exist!
While he is thus exerting himself and striving, others slay him and finish him off; with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the hell named ‘The Vanquished.’”
But if he holds such a view as this:
"When a horseman exerts himself and strives in battle, and while he is exerting himself and striving,
others kill him and finish him off, then with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of the Parajita devas,"
That becomes his wrong view.
And for a person with wrong view, headman, I declare one of two destinations:
either hell or the animal realm.”
When this was said, the village headman Assāroha wept and shed tears.
“It was precisely for this reason, headman, that I did not succeed in getting you to say:
‘Enough, headman, let this be; do not ask me this.’”
“I am not weeping, Bhante, because the Blessed One has said this to me.
Rather, Bhante, for a long time I have been led astray, deceived, and deluded by former teachers and preceptors who were horse-riders, [who taught]:

‘That horse-rider who exerts himself and strives in battle—if others kill him while he is exerting himself and striving, or cause him to perish, then with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of the Parajita devas.’”
“Excellent, Bhante!
… [as before] … From this day forth, for as long as life shall last, we go for refuge.
Thus ends the fifth [discourse].

Saṁyutta Nikāya 42.6 (SN 42.6, PTS SN iv 311) 1. Gāmaṇivagga Asibandhakaputtasutta At Sāvatthī. Then the brahmin Asibandhakaputta approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their polite conversation and greetings, he sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, what is the cause, what is the reason, why among human beings some are short-lived and some long-lived; some have much sickness and some little sickness; some are ugly and some beautiful; some are low-born and some high-born; some are poor and some wealthy; some are lowly and some influential? For it is seen that among human beings some are short-lived and some long-lived; some have much sickness and some little sickness; some are ugly and some beautiful; some are low-born and some high-born; some are poor and some wealthy; some are lowly and some influential. “Brahmin, beings are owners of their kamma, heirs to their kamma, born of their kamma, bound to their kamma, and have kamma as their refuge. It is kamma that distinguishes beings as inferior and superior. “But, Master Gotama, how does one become short-lived through kamma? How does one become long-lived through kamma? How does one become sickly through kamma? How does one become healthy through kamma? How does one become ugly through kamma? How does one become beautiful through kamma? How does one become low-born through kamma? How does one become high-born through kamma? How does one become poor through kamma? How does one become wealthy through kamma? How does one become lowly through kamma? How does one become influential through kamma? “Brahmin, here someone kills living beings, takes what is not given, commits sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. Because of performing and accumulating such kamma, when he passes away, he is reborn in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, even in hell. But if, instead, he comes back to the human state, then wherever he is reborn he is short-lived. This is how one becomes short-lived through kamma. But here, brahmin, someone abstains from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, from sexual misconduct, from false speech, and from liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for negligence. Because of performing and accumulating such kamma, when he passes away, he is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. But if, instead, he comes back to the human state, then wherever he is reborn he is long-lived. This is how one becomes long-lived through kamma. Furthermore, brahmin, here someone is given to injuring beings with the hand, with a clod, with a stick, or with a knife. Because of performing and accumulating such kamma, when he passes away, he is reborn in a state of deprivation… But if, instead, he comes back to the human state, then wherever he is reborn he has much sickness. This is how one becomes sickly through kamma. But here, brahmin, someone is not given to injuring beings with the hand, with a clod, with a stick, or with a knife. Because of performing and accumulating such kamma, when he passes away, he is reborn in a good destination… But if, instead, he comes back to the human state, then wherever he is reborn he has little sickness. This is how one becomes healthy through kamma. Furthermore, brahmin, here someone is angry and bitter, and he harbors anger and bitterness. Because of performing and accumulating such kamma, when he passes away, he is reborn in a state of deprivation… But if, instead, he comes back to the human state, then wherever he is reborn he is ugly. This is how one becomes ugly through kamma. But here, brahmin, someone is not angry and bitter, and he does not harbor anger and bitterness. Because of performing and accumulating such kamma, when he passes away, he is reborn in a good destination… But if, instead, he comes back to the human state, then wherever he is reborn he is beautiful. This is how one becomes beautiful through kamma. Furthermore, brahmin, here someone is envious and avaricious, and he harbors envy and avarice. Because of performing and accumulating such kamma, when he passes away, he is reborn in a state of deprivation… But if, instead, he comes back to the human state, then wherever he is reborn he is low-born. This is how one becomes low-born through kamma. But here, brahmin, someone is not envious and avaricious, and he does not harbor envy and avarice. Because of performing and accumulating such kamma, when he passes away, he is reborn in a good destination… But if, instead, he comes back to the human state, then wherever he is reborn he is high-born. This is how one becomes high-born through kamma. Furthermore, brahmin, here someone is miserly in his own home, and he does not give food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, or lamps to others. Because of performing and accumulating such kamma, when he passes away, he is reborn in a state of deprivation… But if, instead, he comes back to the human state, then wherever he is reborn he is poor. This is how one becomes poor through kamma. But here, brahmin, someone is not miserly in his own home, and he gives food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps to others. Because of performing and accumulating such kamma, when he passes away, he is reborn in a good destination… But if, instead, he comes back to the human state, then wherever he is reborn he is wealthy. This is how one becomes wealthy through kamma. Furthermore, brahmin, here someone is obstinate and arrogant, and he does not pay homage to those who should receive homage, does not rise up for those in whose presence one should rise up, does not offer a seat to those who deserve a seat, and does not make way for those for whom one should make way. Because of performing and accumulating such kamma, when he passes away, he is reborn in a state of deprivation… But if, instead, he comes back to the human state, then wherever he is reborn he is lowly. This is how one becomes lowly through kamma. But here, brahmin, someone is not obstinate and arrogant, and he pays homage to those who should receive homage, rises up for those in whose presence one should rise up, offers a seat to those who deserve a seat, and makes way for those for whom one should make way.

Because of performing and accumulating such kamma, when he passes away, he is reborn in a good destination… But if, instead, he comes back to the human state, then wherever he is reborn he is influential. This is how one becomes influential through kamma. When this was said, the brahmin Asibandhakaputta said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! Just as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to carry a lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes could see forms, in the same way has Master Gotama explained the Dhamma in various ways. I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts. “Brahmin, one who has just gone for refuge should not be admitted [to the Saṅgha]. Wait until you have been trained in the training of the disciples. “Master Gotama, I am already trained in the training of the disciples. For my father’s family, the Asibandhakas, are brahmins learned in the Three Vedas, performers of sacrifices and officiants at sacrifices, teachers of the hymns, expounders of the hymns, and those to whom the hymns have been handed down by oral tradition from teacher to pupil over the course of generations; and my mother’s family, the Todeyyas, are also brahmins learned in the Three Vedas, performers of sacrifices and officiants at sacrifices, teachers of the hymns, expounders of the hymns, and those to whom the hymns have been handed down by oral tradition from teacher to pupil over the course of generations. Both families have for generations been supporters of the Ājīvaka Nigaṇṭhas, yet they have never before sent us to visit any ascetic or brahmin. But now, having heard Master Gotama’s Dhamma, we shall send them to visit Master Gotama from time to time. Then the brahmin Asibandhakaputta, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Nāḷandā in the Pāvārika Mango Grove.
Then Asibandhakaputta the headman approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Asibandhakaputta the headman said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, there are brahmins from the western lands who carry water-pots, wear garlands of water-moss, descend into the water, and tend the sacred fire.
They claim to lead the dead who have passed away out [of this world], to make them recognize [the way], and to cause them to enter heaven.

But is it possible, venerable sir, for the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, to act in such a way that the entire world, upon the breakup of the body after death, would be reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world?”
“In that case, headman, I shall question you about this very matter. Answer as you see fit.
What do you think, headman?

Suppose there were a man here who would take life, take what is not given, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsehoods, speak maliciously, speak harshly, indulge in idle chatter, be covetous, have a mind of ill will, and hold wrong view.”
A great crowd of people would gather together, assemble, entreat him, praise him, and circumambulate him with palms joined, saying:
"May this man, with the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.
What do you think, headman?

“Would that man, because of the great crowd of people’s entreaties, or their praises, or their circumambulations with palms joined, be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, after the breakup of the body, after death?
“No, venerable sir.
“Suppose, headman, a man were to throw a large, thick stone into a deep pool of water.”
Then a great crowd of people, having gathered and assembled, would entreat it, praise it, and circumambulate it with palms joined, saying:
‘Arise, O large stone! Float up, O large stone! Float onto dry land, O large stone!
What do you think, headman?

“Would that large boulder, because of the entreaties of the great crowd of people, or because of their praises, or because of their circumambulating with palms joined, rise up, float up, or even wash ashore?
“No indeed, Bhante.

“In the same way, headman, consider a person who destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehoods, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, indulges in idle chatter, is covetous, has a mind of ill will, and holds wrong view.”
Even though that great mass of people, having gathered and assembled together, should entreat him, praise him, and circumambulate him with palms joined, saying:

“May this person, upon the breakup of the body after death, be reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world,” yet that person, upon the breakup of the body after death, might still be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, or hell.
What do you think, headman?
Here, a person abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct,
abstains from false speech, abstains from malicious speech, abstains from harsh speech, and abstains from idle chatter;
he is free from covetousness, has a mind without ill will, and possesses right view.
A great crowd of people would gather together and, with palms joined, would entreat, praise, and circumambulate him, saying:
‘May this man, upon the breakup of the body after death, be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell.
What do you think, headman?

“Would that man, because of the entreaties, praises, or the circumambulations with palms joined by the great multitude of people, be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell after the breakup of the body, after death?
“No indeed, Bhante.
“Just as if, headman, a man were to sink a jar of ghee or a jar of oil into a deep pool of water...”
It would break. Therein, whatever gravel or pebbles it contained would go downward, while whatever ghee or oil it contained would rise upward.
Then a great crowd of people, having gathered and assembled, would entreat it, praise it, and circumambulate it with palms joined in reverence:
“Sink down, sir, ghee and oil! Sunk down, sir, ghee and oil! Go downwards, sir, ghee and oil!

What do you think, headman, would that ghee and oil sink down, or sink further, or go downwards because of the great crowd of people’s entreaties, praises, or their circumambulating with palms joined?”
“No, venerable sir. “In the same way, headman, that person who abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given,
abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from malicious speech...”
“Abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter, free from covetousness, with a mind devoid of ill will, and possessing right view—
even if that great multitude of people were to gather together, assemble, entreat him, praise him, and circumambulate him with palms joined, saying: ‘May this person,

upon the breakup of the body after death, be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, ruin, or hell’— nevertheless, that person, upon the breakup of the body after death, would be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.”
When this was said, Asibandhakaputta the headman said to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Bhante! ... [as before] ...
From today forth, for as long as life shall last, I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.”
The Sixth.

The Discourse on the Simile of the Field.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Nālandā in Pāvārika’s Mango Grove.
Then Asibandhakaputta the headman approached the Blessed One; having approached, he [greeted] the Blessed One...
Having paid homage, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Asibandhakaputta the headman said to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, does the Blessed One not dwell compassionate toward all living beings?
“It is so, headman; the Tathāgata dwells compassionate toward all living beings.”
“But why is it, venerable sir, that the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma thoroughly to some, yet does not teach the Dhamma so thoroughly to others?
“In that case, headman, I shall question you about this very matter. Answer as you see fit.
What do you think, headman? Suppose there were a householder farmer with three fields: one field excellent, one field middling, and one field inferior—a wasteland, saline, and poor soil.”
“What do you think, headman? When that farmer householder wishes to plant seeds, where would he plant them first:
in that field which is the best, or that field which is middling, or that field which is inferior—a wasteland, saline, and a piece of bad ground?”
“Venerable sir, suppose that farmer, wishing to plant seeds, would first plant them in that field which is the best;
having planted them there, he would then plant them in that field which is middling;
having planted them there, he might or might not even plant them in that field which is inferior—a wasteland, saline, and a piece of bad ground.
"And for what reason?
Because there will be at least enough for cow-feed.
"Just as that field is the best, Gāmaṇi, even so are my monks and nuns."
To them I teach the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end—with the right meaning and phrasing; I proclaim the holy life in its entirety, perfectly pure.
And why is that? Because, headman, they dwell with me as their island, with me as their shelter, with me as their protection, and with me as their refuge.
"Just as that field is middling, so too are my male and female lay followers.

To them I teach the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; I proclaim the holy life in its entirety, perfectly pure. And why is that?"
"For these, headman, dwell with me as their island, with me as their shelter, with me as their protection, and with me as their refuge.
Just as that field, headman, might be inferior, wild, saline, and a wasteland, even so are the ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers of other sects to me.
To them I teach the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; I proclaim the holy life in its entirety, perfectly pure."
And why is that? Because perhaps they might understand even a single verse, which would be for their long-term welfare and happiness.

It is just as if, headman, a man had three water-jars: one water-jar that was without cracks, neither leaking nor seeping; one water-jar that was without cracks, leaking but not seeping; and one water-jar that was cracked, both leaking and seeping.
"What do you think, headman? If that man wished to set down water, where would he set it down first:
in the water-jar that was without cracks, leak-proof, and not leaking; or in the water-jar that was without cracks, leaking, but not leaking away;
or in the water-jar that was cracked, leaking, and leaking away?"
“Venerable sir, suppose a man wishing to set down water were to pour it into a water-jar that is without cracks, yet leaks and is porous;
having poured it there, he were then to pour it into a water-jar that is without cracks and leaks, yet is porous;
and having poured it there, he were then to pour it into a water-jar that is cracked, leaks, and is porous...”
"He might set it down, or he might not set it down.
And why? Because there will even be the washing of the goods."
“Just as, headman, that water-jar is without cracks, without leaks, and without holes, even so are my monks and nuns.
To them I teach the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; I proclaim the holy life in its entirety, perfectly pure.
And for what reason?
"For these, headman, dwell with me as their island, with me as their shelter, with me as their protection, and with me as their refuge.
Just as that water-jar, headman, is without cracks, leak-proof, and watertight, even so are my male and female lay followers.
To them I teach the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; I proclaim the holy life in its entirety, perfectly pure."
For what reason?
Because, headman, these others dwell with me as their island, me as their shelter, me as their protection, and me as their refuge.
Just as that water-jar, headman, which is cracked, leaking, and porous, even so are the ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers of other sects in relation to me.
To them I teach the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; I reveal the holy life, entirely complete and pure.
And for what reason?
So that they might perhaps understand even a single verse, which would be for their welfare and happiness for a long time.”
When this was said, Asibandhakaputta the headman said to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Bhante! Magnificent, Bhante!
… [as before] … May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.”
The Seventh.

The Discourse on the Conch-Blower On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Nāḷandā in Pāvārika’s Mango Grove.

Then Asibandhakaputta the headman, a disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he sat down to one side. As Asibandhakaputta the headman was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“How, headman, does the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta teach the Dhamma to his disciples?
“Venerable sir, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta teaches the Dhamma to his disciples in this way:
‘Whoever destroys life, all such are destined for states of deprivation, for hell; whoever takes what is not given, all such...’”

"He is destined for states of deprivation, destined for hell—whosoever engages in sexual misconduct among sensual pleasures, all such persons are destined for states of deprivation, destined for hell;
whosoever speaks falsehood, all such persons are destined for states of deprivation, destined for hell.
To whatever extent one dwells predominantly in a certain state, by that very state is one led."
“In this way, Bhante, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta teaches the Dhamma to his disciples.

“If, headman, one is led here and there by whatever one frequently dwells upon, then according to the word of the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, no one at all would be destined for states of deprivation or rebirth in hell.
What do you think, headman?”

“Take that man who is a killer of living beings: whether by night or by day, considering the intervals of time, which period is greater—the time during which he kills a living being, or the time during which he does not kill a living being?
“Venerable sir, take that man who is a killer of living beings: whether by night or by day, considering the intervals of time, the time during which he kills a living being is smaller;
rather, that very time during which he does not kill a living being is greater.”

“‘Gāmaṇi, one is led by whatever one dwells upon most frequently,’ if this were so, then according to the word of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, no one would ever be destined for a state of deprivation or reborn in hell.
What do you think, Gāmaṇi?

Regarding that man who takes what is not given, whether by night or by day, depending on the time or the non-time, which is more frequent: the occasion when he takes what is not given, or the occasion when he does not take what is not given?”
“Venerable sir, for that person who takes what is not given, whether by night or by day, the occasion on which he takes what is not given is less frequent;
rather, the occasion on which he does not take what is not given is much more frequent.

“If it is true, headman, that ‘one is led away according to whatever one dwells upon most frequently,’ then, this being the case, no one at all would be bound for a state of misery or reborn in hell, according to the word of the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.”
“What do you think, headman? For that man who engages in sexual misconduct by day or by night, depending on the time and non-time, which period is greater:
the time when he engages in sexual misconduct, or the time when he does not engage in sexual misconduct?”
“Venerable sir, for that person who engages in sexual misconduct, whether by night or by day,
depending on the time and non-time, the time during which he engages in sexual misconduct is less, whereas the time during which he does not engage in sexual misconduct is much more.”

“‘Whatever one dwells upon frequently, headman, by that one is led away’—if this were so, then according to the word of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, no one would ever be bound for a state of misery or reborn in hell.

What do you think, headman: for a person who is a liar, whether by night or by day, depending on the occasion or non-occasion, which is more frequent—the time when he speaks falsely, or the time when he does not speak falsely?”

“Venerable sir, for that person who speaks falsehood, whether by night or by day, depending on the time and the non-time, the time during which he speaks falsehood is shorter; rather, the time during which he does not speak falsehood is much longer.

“If it were as you say, ‘Gāmaṇi, one is led away by whatever one dwells upon most frequently,’ then according to the word of the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, no one at all would be destined for states of deprivation or hell.
But here, Gāmaṇi, a certain teacher holds such a doctrine and such a view:”

‘Whoever destroys living beings, all such are destined for states of deprivation, destined for hell; whoever takes what is not given, all such are destined for states of deprivation, destined for hell;
whoever engages in sexual misconduct, all such are destined for states of deprivation, destined for hell;
whoever speaks falsehood, all such are destined for states of deprivation, destined for hell.’
Furthermore, headman, a disciple has full confidence in that Teacher.
It occurs to him:
"My Teacher speaks thus and holds such a view:..."
"Whoever takes the life of a living being, all such persons are destined for states of deprivation, for hell.
One then acquires the view: "I have indeed taken the life of a living being; I too am destined for states of deprivation, for hell.
Without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that thought, and without relinquishing that view, O headman, one is placed in hell just as if carried there.
"My teacher indeed speaks thus and holds this view:
'Whoever takes what is not given, all such persons are destined for states of misery, for hell.
Yet, having taken what was not given by me, I acquire the view: 'I too am destined for states of misery, for hell.'"
“Headman, if one does not abandon that speech, does not abandon that mind, and does not relinquish that view, one will be placed in hell just as if one had been carried there.
My Teacher, however, speaks thus and holds this view:
‘Whoever engages in sexual misconduct among sensual pleasures, all such persons are destined for the states of deprivation and hell.’”
"However, there is indeed wrong conduct by me regarding sensual pleasures.
One acquires the view: 'I too am destined for the states of deprivation, destined for hell.
Without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that mind, and without relinquishing that view, O headman, one is placed in hell just as if carried there."
"My teacher indeed holds this doctrine and this view:
'Whoever speaks falsely, all such persons are destined for states of deprivation and hell.
Yet, I have spoken falsely."
‘I am one bound for the states of deprivation, bound for hell,’ he acquires such a view.
Without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that thought, and without relinquishing that view, Gāmaṇi, he is placed in hell just as he was brought there.

But here, Gāmaṇi, a Tathāgata arises in the world—an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, well-gone, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
Thus, in many ways, he censures and rebukes the taking of life, saying, "Abstain from taking life.
He censures and rebukes the taking of what is not given, saying, "Abstain from taking what is not given.
He censures sexual misconduct, saying, "Abstain from sexual misconduct."
He censures and reproaches false speech, saying, “Abstain from false speech!
And, headman, a disciple has full confidence in that Teacher.
He reflects thus:
“The Blessed One has, in many ways, censured and rebuked the taking of life, saying, ‘Abstain from taking life.
Yet, I have taken life, whether it was much or little.
Whatever life I have taken, whether much or little—that was not good; that was not right.”
‘If I were to feel remorse because of that,
this evil deed would not have been undone by me.
Having reflected thus, he abandons that very act of taking life.
And in the future, he abstains from the destruction of life.
In this way, there is the abandoning of this evil karma;
in this way, there is the transcending of this evil karma.
“The Blessed One, indeed, in many ways censures and reproves the taking of what is not given, and he says: ‘Abstain from taking what is not given.
Yet there is something taken by me that was not given, whether much or little.
Whatever has been taken by me that was not given, whether much or little—that was not well done; that was not good.”
‘If, on account of this, I should feel remorse, this evil deed will not have been undone.
Having reflected thus, he abandons that very act of taking what is not given and,
in the future, abstains from taking what is not given.
In this way, there is the abandoning of this evil karma;
in this way, there is the transcending of this evil karma.
Furthermore, the Blessed One has in many ways censured and rebuked sexual misconduct, and he has said: "Abstain from sexual misconduct."
‘Indeed, I have engaged in sexual misconduct to whatever extent;
and whatever sexual misconduct I have engaged in, to whatever extent, that was neither well done nor good.
If I were to feel remorse because of that, this evil deed would not remain undone.’”
Having reflected thus, he abandons that very sexual misconduct and, in the future, refrains from sexual misconduct.
In this way, there is the abandoning of that evil deed;
in this way, there is the transcending of that evil deed.
‘The Blessed One indeed censures and rebukes false speech in many ways, saying, “Abstain from false speech!
Yet there is some false speech that has been spoken by me, whether much or little.

Whatever false speech has been spoken by me, whether much or little, that was not well done; that was not good. If I were to feel remorse because of that, this evil deed would not have remained undone.’
Having reflected thus, he abandons that very false speech and becomes one who abstains from false speech in the future.
In this way, there is the abandoning of this evil deed; in this way, there is the transcending of this evil deed.
Having abandoned the destruction of life, he becomes one who abstains from the destruction of life.
Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given.
Having abandoned sexual misconduct, he abstains from sexual misconduct.
Having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false speech.
Having abandoned divisive speech, he abstains from divisive speech.
Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech.
Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter.
Having abandoned covetousness, he becomes free from covetousness.
Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he becomes one whose mind is free from malice.
Having abandoned wrong view, he becomes one who possesses right view.

In this way, headman, that noble disciple—free from covetousness, free from ill will, undeluded, clearly comprehending, and mindful—dwells having pervaded one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness;

likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, and everywhere, to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness.
He dwells having pervaded the world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness— vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will. Just as, headman,
a powerful conch-blower might easily make himself heard in all four directions, even so, headman,
when the liberation of mind through loving-kindness has been developed and cultivated in this way, whatever action is limited does not remain there, nor does it persist there.

In this way, headman, that noble disciple—free from covetousness, free from ill will, undeluded, clearly comprehending, and mindful—dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with compassion...
[and so on] ...with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy...
[and so on] ...with a mind imbued with equanimity; likewise the second, likewise the third, [and the fourth].

And so it was with the fourth. Thus, above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells having pervaded the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
Just as, headman, a powerful conch-blower might easily make himself heard in the four directions;
“In the same way, headman, when the liberation of mind through equanimity has been developed and cultivated in this way, any action that is measurable will neither remain there nor persist there.
When this was said, Asibandhakaputta the headman said to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! …” [as above] …
“May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
The eighth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 42.9 (SN 42.9, PTS SN iv 322)
1. Gāmaṇivagga, Kulasutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One, while wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus, arrived at Nāḷandā.
At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Nāḷandā in the Pāvārika mango grove.
Now, at that time, Nāḷandā was suffering from a famine—scarcity of food, with crops blighted by drought and reduced to mere stalks.
At that same time, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta was residing in Nāḷandā together with a large assembly of Nigaṇṭhas.
Then Asibandhakaputta the headman, a disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas, approached the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta;
having approached, he paid homage to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said this to Asibandhakaputta the headman:
“Come now, headman, refute the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama.
In this way, a fine report of your reputation will spread abroad:
‘The headman Asibandhakaputta has refuted the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama, who possesses such great psychic power and such great majesty.’”
“But how, venerable sir, shall I refute the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama, who possesses such great psychic power and such great majesty?
“Come now, headman, go to where the ascetic Gotama is; having approached him, say this to the ascetic Gotama:
‘Venerable sir, does not the Blessed One in many ways praise compassion for families, praise protection [of families], and praise sympathy [for families]?’”
“If, headman, the ascetic Gotama, being asked thus, answers thus:
‘It is so, headman; in many ways the Tathāgata praises compassion for families, praises protection, and praises sympathy,’ then you should say to him:

‘But why, venerable sir, does the Blessed One travel on tour with a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus at a time of famine, when there are only two crops, when stalks are white, and when food is measured out with sticks?’”
“The Blessed One is practicing for the destruction of families; the Blessed One is practicing for the ruin of families; the Blessed One is practicing for the harm of families.
“In this way, headman, when the ascetic Gotama is asked this double-edged question, he will be unable neither to spit it out nor to swallow it down.
“Yes, venerable sir,” Asibandhakaputta the headman replied to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.
Rising from his seat, he paid homage to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Asibandhakaputta the headman said this to the Blessed One:
“But, Bhante, does not the Blessed One in many ways praise compassion for families, praise protection for families, and praise sympathy for families?
“Yes, headman, the Tathāgata in many ways praises compassion for families, praises protection for families, and praises sympathy for families.

“Then why, Bhante, does the Blessed One now wander on tour with a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus through a time of famine, when there are only two crops, when stalks are white, and when food is distributed by tally-sticks?”
“The Blessed One practices for the destruction of families; the Blessed One practices for the ruin of families; the Blessed One practices for the injury of families.
“Gāmaṇi, as far back as I recollect ninety-one aeons from now, I do not recall any family that has ever been ruined merely by the offering of cooked almsfood.
On the contrary, those families which were wealthy, affluent, and possessed of great riches, with abundant gold and silver—”
Abundant wealth and requisites, abundant riches and grain— all these arise from giving, arise from truth,
and arise from the life of a recluse.
Furthermore, headman, there are eight causes and eight conditions for the ruin of families.
Families come to ruin through kings, or families come to ruin through thieves, or families come to ruin through fire,
or families come to ruin through water; or what has been stored away disappears from its place,
or undertakings fail due to being poorly managed, or a family calamity arises within the family.
"Whoever scatters, disperses, and destroys your wealth does so because of impermanence itself;
such is the eighth [cause]. "These, headman, are the eight causes and eight conditions for the ruin of families.
When these eight causes and eight conditions are present, whoever should say of me:"
“The Blessed One practices for the destruction of families; the Blessed One practices for the ruin of families; the Blessed One practices for the harm of families.
If, headman, one does not abandon that speech, does not abandon that mind, and does not relinquish that view, then one will be placed in hell just like the carrying of a load.
When this was said, Asibandhakaputta the headman said this to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Bhante! Magnificent, Bhante!
… [as before] … May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
The ninth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 42.10 (SN 42.10, PTS SN iv 325) 1. Gāmaṇivagga Maṇicūḷakasutta At Sāvatthī. Then the brahmin Maṇicūḷaka approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their greetings and cordial talk, he sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The one who torments himself and pursues the practice of torturing himself; the one who torments others and pursues the practice of torturing others; the one who torments himself and pursues the practice of torturing himself as well as others; and the one who neither torments himself nor pursues the practice of torturing himself, nor torments others nor pursues the practice of torturing others, but dwells having transcended both self-torment and the torment of others, and who, through the destruction of the taints, enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, realizing it for himself with direct knowledge. These are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. When this was said, the Blessed One asked the brahmin Maṇicūḷaka: “Brahmin, what kind of person is the one who torments himself and pursues the practice of torturing himself? “The one who goes without clothes, who plucks out his hair and beard, who subsists on water, who eats only once every day, who eats only once every two days… who eats only once every seven days, or even longer; who lives on fallen leaves, on broken rice, on rice-scum, on moss, on the flour of oilseeds, on rice-water, on grass, on cow dung, on forest roots and fruits, or who clothes himself in bark garments, in antelope hides, in strips of cloth, in kusa-grass garments, in bark-shavings garments, in animal-blanket coverings, in bird-feather garments, or in garments of human hair, or of horse-hair, or of owls’ wings; who stands continuously, who squats continuously, who uses a mattress of thorns, who makes his bed on a mattress of thorns, who dwells intent on the practice of exposing himself to the cold, who dwells intent on the practice of exposure to the heat, who dwells intent on the practice of facing the sun, who dwells intent on the practice of living in the open air, who dwells intent on the practice of living in a charnel ground, who sleeps wherever he happens to be, who always speaks the truth, who always stands, who never sits down, who never lies down, or who has such a custom as this: ‘Whenever anyone asks me anything, I answer, but if no one asks me anything, I do not speak at all. This, Master Gotama, is the kind of person who torments himself and pursues the practice of torturing himself. “But, brahmin, is that the only way in which a person torments himself and pursues the practice of torturing himself? “No, Master Gotama. There is another way. “And what is that way? “Here, Master Gotama, someone eats only one bean a day… one grain of rice a day… one drop of ghee a day… one drop of oil a day… one drop of honey a day… one drop of molasses a day… he eats only one fiber of jute a day… he eats only one fiber of hemp a day… he eats only one fiber of bark a day… he eats only one fiber of grass a day… he eats only one fiber of wood a day… he eats only one fiber of cow dung a day… he eats only one grain of rice, one bean, one mustard seed a day… he eats only once a day… once every two days… once every three days… once every four days… once every five days… once every six days… once every seven days, or even longer; he dwells intent on the practice of exposing himself to the cold, the heat, and the wind; he dwells intent on the practice of standing continuously and squatting continuously; he dwells intent on the practice of facing the sun, living in the open air, and living in a charnel ground; he sleeps wherever he happens to be, or adopts such a custom as this: ‘Whenever anyone asks me anything, I answer, but if no one asks me anything, I do not speak at all. This, Master Gotama, is the kind of person who torments himself and pursues the practice of torturing himself. “But, brahmin, is that the only way in which a person torments himself and pursues the practice of torturing himself? “No, Master Gotama. There is another way. “And what is that way?

“Here, Master Gotama, someone smears his body with ashes, or with mud, or with dirt, or with dust, or with salt, or with mustard seeds, or with gravel, or with pebbles, or with iron filings, or with sand, or with charcoal powder, or with lime, or with clay, or with cow dung; he pierces his body with wooden stakes, or with bamboo splinters, or with thorns, or with iron spikes, or with arrows; he cuts his flesh with razors, or with knives, or with axes; he gashes his body with sharp weapons; he leaps from high places; he enters fire; he practices the vow of the dog, or the vow of the ox, or the vow of the deer, or the vow of the cock, or the vow of the dog’s ways, or the vow of the ox’s ways, or the vow of the deer’s ways, or the vow of the cock’s ways; he dwells intent on the practice of exposing himself to the cold, the heat, and the wind; he dwells intent on the practice of standing continuously and squatting continuously; he dwells intent on the practice of facing the sun, living in the open air, and living in a charnel ground; he sleeps wherever he happens to be, or adopts such a custom as this: ‘Whenever anyone asks me anything, I answer, but if no one asks me anything, I do not speak at all. This, Master Gotama, is the kind of person who torments himself and pursues the practice of torturing himself. “But, brahmin, is that the only way in which a person torments himself and pursues the practice of torturing himself? “No, Master Gotama. There is another way. “And what is that way? “Here, Master Gotama, someone undergoes the initiation of a fire-worshipper, undergoing the initiation for twelve years. Having undergone the initiation of a fire-worshipper for twelve years, he then becomes a student of the Vedas, undergoing the initiation for twelve years. Having become a student of the Vedas for twelve years, he then becomes a householder, undergoing the initiation for twelve years. Having become a householder for twelve years, he then becomes a forest-dweller, undergoing the initiation for twelve years. Having become a forest-dweller for twelve years, he then becomes a wanderer, undergoing the initiation for twelve years. Having become a wanderer for twelve years, he then becomes a naked ascetic, undergoing the initiation for twelve years.
