On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, while the royal assembly was sitting together and gathered in the royal palace, this discussion arose among them:

“Is it permissible for the ascetics who follow the son of the Sakyans to accept gold and silver? Do the ascetics who follow the son of the Sakyans consent to gold and silver? Do the ascetics who follow the son of the Sakyans receive gold and silver?”
Now at that time, Maṇicūḷaka the village headman was seated in that assembly.
Then Maṇicūḷaka the village headman said this to that assembly:
"Sirs, do not speak thus."
“Gold and silver are not allowable for the recluses, sons of the Sakyans;

the recluses, sons of the Sakyans, do not accept gold and silver, they do not take hold of gold and silver; the recluses, sons of the Sakyans, have laid aside gems and gold, and are free from gold and silver.”
Maṇicūḷaka the headman was able to convince that assembly.

Then Maṇicūḷaka the headman approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Maṇicūḷaka the headman said this to the Blessed One:
“Just now, Bhante, while the royal assembly was sitting together and gathered in the royal palace, this discussion arose among them:”
‘Gold and silver are allowable for the recluses, sons of the Sakyans; the recluses, sons of the Sakyans, accept gold and silver; the recluses, sons of the Sakyans, receive gold and silver.
When this was said, venerable sir, I said to that assembly:
‘Noble sirs, do not speak thus.’”
"It is not permissible for the ascetics who are followers of the Sakyan to [accept] gold and silver;

the ascetics who are followers of the Sakyan do not consent to gold and silver, they do not receive gold and silver; the ascetics who are followers of the Sakyan have laid aside gems and gold, and are free from gold and silver."
"I was indeed able, Bhante, to convince that assembly.
In answering thus, Bhante, am I one who speaks in accordance with what has been said by the Blessed One? Do I not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is false?
Do I explain in accordance with the Dhamma, such that no one who follows the Dhamma could reasonably object?"
“Does a legitimate ground for censure arise from such a statement?
“Indeed, headman, by answering thus you have spoken exactly as I have said;
you do not misrepresent me with what is untrue, you explain in accordance with the Dhamma, and no one can reasonably challenge you with a counter-argument based on the Dhamma.”
One falls into a blameworthy position.
For indeed, headman, it is not permissible for the recluses, sons of the Sakyan, to accept gold and silver;
the recluses, sons of the Sakyan, do not consent to gold and silver, nor do they receive gold and silver.
"The ascetics, sons of the Sakyan, have laid aside jewels and gold; they are free from bullion and silver.
Headman, for whomsoever bullion and silver are permissible, for him the five strands of sensual pleasure are also permissible.
For whomsoever the five strands of sensual pleasure are permissible, headman, you may categorically conclude: 'This is not the dharma of an ascetic, this is not the dharma of a son of the Sakyan.'"
"Furthermore, headman, I say this:
one who needs grass should seek grass; one who needs wood should seek wood; one who needs a cart should seek a cart; one who needs a man should seek a man.
But by no means whatsoever, headman, do I say that gold and silver should be accepted or sought after."
The Tenth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 42.11 (SN 42.11, PTS SN iv 327) 1.
Gāmaṇivagga (The Chapter on Village Chiefs)
The Bhadraka Sutta On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Mallans at a town of the Mallans named Uruvelakappa.

Then Bhadraka the headman approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Bhadraka the headman said this to the Blessed One:
“It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the origin and the passing away of suffering.
“If, headman, I were to teach you the origin and the passing away of suffering with reference to the past,
saying, ‘Thus it was in the past,’ there might be perplexity in you, there might be doubt.”
“Gāmaṇi, if I were to teach you the origin and the passing away of suffering concerning the future time,
saying, ‘Thus it will be in the future,’ there might still be doubt and uncertainty in you regarding that.
However, Gāmaṇi, while sitting right here, I shall teach you the origin and the passing away of suffering for you who are sitting right here.”
“Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” Bhadraka the headman replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“What do you think, headman?
Are there any people in Uruvelakappa for whom, through their execution, imprisonment, loss of wealth, or censure, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would arise in you?
“There are, Bhante, some people in Uruvelakappa for whom, through their execution, imprisonment, loss of wealth, or censure, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would arise in me.”
“But, headman, are there people in Uruvelakappa for whom, through your execution, imprisonment, ruin, or censure, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise?
“There are, Bhante, people in Uruvelakappa for whom, through my execution, imprisonment, ruin, or censure, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise.”

“Headman, what is the cause, what is the reason, why sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair might arise for you upon the killing, imprisonment, loss, or censure of certain people from Uruvelakappa?

“Venerable sir, it is because there is desire and lust for those people from Uruvelakappa that sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would arise for me upon their killing, imprisonment, loss, or censure.”
“But, Bhante, regarding those people of Uruvelakappa for whose killing, imprisonment, ruin, or censure sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise—in them I have no desire or lust.
“In this way, headman, by means of this Dhamma that is seen, known, attained, fathomed, and not subject to time, apply the method to the past and the future:

‘Whatever suffering arose at any time in the past, all that was rooted in desire, had its source in desire. Whatever suffering will arise at any time in the future, all that will be rooted in desire, will have its source in desire.’”
"For desire is the root of suffering.
Whatever suffering will arise at some time in the future, all that has desire as its root, desire as its source.
For desire is the root of suffering."
“It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir!
How well this has been stated by the Blessed One:
‘Whatever suffering arises, all that arises rooted in desire, with desire as its source.’”
"For desire is indeed the root of suffering.
"Venerable sir, I have a young man named Ciravāsi who lives in a residence outside [the city].
Rising early, venerable sir, I dispatch a man with the message:"
“Go, my man, and find out about Prince Ciravāsi.
“Venerable sir, as long as that man has not returned, I am indeed anxious, thinking:
‘May nothing have happened to harm Prince Ciravāsi.’”
“What do you think, headman?
Would sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise for Ciravāsi the youth because of his execution, imprisonment, loss, or censure?

“Venerable sir, if Ciravāsi the youth were to suffer execution, imprisonment, loss, or censure, even my own life would be changed; how much more so would sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair not arise for me?”
“In this way too, headman, it should be understood:
‘Whatever suffering arises, all that arises rooted in desire, with desire as its source.
For desire is the root of suffering.’”
“What do you think, headman?
When Ciravāsi’s mother was neither seen nor heard by you, did you have any desire, lust, or affection for Ciravāsi’s mother?
“No indeed, Bhante.”
“Did it occur to you, headman, after seeing or hearing [her],
‘There is desire, lust, or affection for Ciravāsi’s mother’?”—
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“What do you think, headman?
Upon the execution, imprisonment, loss, or censure of Ciravāsi’s mother, would sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise in you?
“Venerable sir, upon the execution, imprisonment, loss, or censure of Ciravāsi’s mother, even my very life might change; how then could sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair not arise in me?”
“By this method, too, headman, it should be understood:
‘Whatever suffering arises, all that arises rooted in desire, with desire as its source.
For desire is the root of suffering.’”
The Eleventh.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 42.12 (SN 42.12, PTS SN iv 330) 1.
The Chapter on Village Chiefs (Gāmaṇivagga)

The Discourse to Rāsiya Then Rāsiya the village headman approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Rāsiya the village headman said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I have heard this: ‘The ascetic Gotama censures all austerity; he single-mindedly reviles and disparages every ascetic who leads a life of hardship.’”
“Venerable sir, as for those who say this: ‘The ascetic Gotama disparages all austerity;
he single-mindedly censures and reviles every ascetic who leads a harsh life’—do they, venerable sir, speak the word of the Blessed One?
Do they not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is false? And do they explain in accordance with the Dhamma, so that their explanation does not lead to harm?”
“Does anyone who engages in a legitimate discussion find grounds for censure?

“Those, headman, who say: ‘The ascetic Gotama disparages all austerity and, with one-sided condemnation, reviles and censures every ascetic who lives a life of hardship’—they do not speak my words; they misrepresent me.”
"Moreover, they have addressed me with what is untrue, empty, and false.
There are these two extremes, headman, that one who has gone forth should not pursue:
the devotion to the pleasure of sense desires, which is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial; and the devotion to self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial."

"Headman, having avoided these two extremes, the Middle Way has been fully realized by the Tathāgata; it produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, full enlightenment, and Nibbāna.
And what, headman, is that Middle Way realized by the Tathāgata which produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, full enlightenment, and Nibbāna?
It is simply this Noble Eightfold Path; namely:"
Right view... [and so on] ...right concentration.
This, headman, is that middle way discovered by the Tathāgata—which produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to self-awakening, and to Nibbāna.
There are, headman, three kinds of enjoyers of sensual pleasures found existing in the world.
Which three?

Here, headman, a certain enjoyer of sensual pleasures seeks wealth unrighteously, by violence. Having sought wealth unrighteously, by violence, he does not make himself happy and pleased, nor does he share it, nor does he perform meritorious deeds.
But here, headman, another enjoyer of sensual pleasures seeks wealth unrighteously, by violence.
Having sought wealth unrighteously and by force, one makes oneself happy and pleased, yet does not share it nor perform meritorious deeds.
But here, headman, some enjoyer of sensual pleasures seeks wealth unrighteously and by force;
having sought wealth unrighteously and by force, he makes himself happy and pleased, and he shares it and performs meritorious deeds.
Furthermore, headman, here a certain enjoyer of sensual pleasures seeks wealth both by lawful and unlawful means, both by violence and without violence.

Having sought wealth both by lawful and unlawful means, both by violence and without violence, he does not make himself happy, nor does he gladden himself; he does not share it, nor does he perform meritorious deeds.
Furthermore, headman, here a certain enjoyer of sensual pleasures seeks wealth both by lawful and unlawful means, both by violence and without violence.

Having sought wealth by both righteous and unrighteous means, and by both violent and non-violent means, one makes oneself happy and pleased, yet does not share it and does not perform meritorious deeds.
But here, headman, a certain enjoyer of sensual pleasures seeks wealth by both righteous and unrighteous means, and by both violent and non-violent means.
Having sought wealth by both righteous and unrighteous means, and by both violent and non-violent means, he makes himself happy and pleased, shares it, and performs meritorious deeds.
But here, headman, a certain enjoyer of sensual pleasures seeks wealth righteously and without violence.
Having sought wealth righteously and without violence, he does not make himself happy, nor does he gladden himself, nor does he share it, nor does he perform meritorious deeds.
But here, headman, another certain enjoyer of sensual pleasures seeks wealth righteously and without violence.
Having sought wealth righteously and without violence, one makes oneself happy and pleased, yet does not share it nor perform meritorious deeds.
But here, headman, some enjoyer of sensual pleasures seeks wealth righteously and without violence;
having sought wealth righteously and without violence, he makes himself happy and pleased, shares it, and performs meritorious deeds.
And he enjoys those riches while being deeply attached to them, infatuated with them, and obsessed by them; he fails to see their danger and lacks wisdom regarding the means of escape from them.
But here, headman, some enjoyer of sensual pleasures seeks wealth righteously and without violence.
Having sought wealth righteously and without violence, he makes himself happy and pleased, shares it with others, and performs meritorious deeds.

And he enjoys those possessions without being attached to them, without being infatuated with them, without being tied to them, seeing their danger and understanding the escape from them. In this regard, headman,

that enjoyer of sensual pleasures who seeks wealth unrighteously and by violence, and having sought wealth unrighteously and by violence, does not gladden himself, does not exhilarate himself, does not share it, and does not perform meritorious deeds—
this enjoyer of sensual pleasures, headman, is to be censured on three grounds.
In what three respects is he censurable?
He seeks wealth unrighteously and by force—this is the first respect in which he is censurable.
He does not make himself happy or joyful—this is the second respect in which he is censurable.
"He does not share [his wealth], nor does he perform meritorious deeds"—on account of this third ground, he is to be censured.
"Gāmaṇi, this enjoyer of sensual pleasures is to be censured for these three grounds.

In that regard, Gāmaṇi, as for the enjoyer of sensual pleasures who seeks wealth unrighteously and by violence, and having sought wealth unrighteously and by violence, makes himself happy and pleased, yet does not share it nor perform meritorious deeds..."
“Headman, this enjoyer of sensual pleasures is to be criticized on two grounds and praised on one ground.
On which two grounds is he to be criticized?
He seeks wealth by what is not the Dhamma and by violence; on this first ground he is to be criticized.”
"He does not share [his wealth] and does not perform meritorious deeds"—on account of this second ground, he is to be censured.
On account of which one ground is he to be praised?
"He makes himself happy and satisfied"—on account of this one ground, he is to be praised.
“Headman, this enjoyer of sensual pleasures is to be criticized for these two reasons and praised for this one reason.

In this regard, headman, as for the enjoyer of sensual pleasures who seeks wealth unrighteously and by violence, and having sought wealth unrighteously and by violence, makes himself happy and pleased, shares it, and performs meritorious deeds—
this enjoyer of sensual pleasures, headman, is to be criticized for one reason and praised for two reasons.”
In what one instance is he to be censured?
He seeks wealth unrighteously and by violence; in this one instance he is to be censured.
In what two instances is he to be praised?
"He makes himself happy and satisfied"—by this first ground he is praiseworthy.
"He shares [his wealth] and performs meritorious deeds"—by this second ground he is praiseworthy.
This enjoyer of sensual pleasures, headman, is to be censured for one ground, but is praiseworthy for these two grounds.
In this regard, headman, there is the enjoyer of sensual pleasures who seeks wealth both righteously and unrighteously, by violence and without violence;
yet having sought wealth both righteously and unrighteously, by violence and without violence, he does not make himself happy,
nor does he gladden himself, nor does he share it, nor does he perform meritorious deeds.
“Headman, this enjoyer of sensual pleasures is praiseworthy in one respect and blameworthy in three respects.
In what one respect is he praiseworthy?
He seeks wealth righteously and without violence; in this one respect he is praiseworthy.”
In what three respects is he censurable?
He seeks wealth unrighteously and by force—this is the first respect in which he is censurable.
He does not make himself happy, nor does he gladden himself—this is the second respect in which he is censurable.
"He does not share [his wealth] and does not perform meritorious deeds"—on account of this third ground, he is to be censured.
Thus, headman, this enjoyer of sensual pleasures is praiseworthy for this one ground and censurable for these three grounds.
In that regard, headman, as for the enjoyer of sensual pleasures who seeks wealth both by lawful and unlawful means, both by violence and without violence:
Having sought wealth both by right means and by wrong means, and both by violent and non-violent means, one makes oneself happy and pleased,
yet does not share it nor perform meritorious deeds.
This enjoyer of sensual pleasures, headman, is praiseworthy in two respects and blameworthy in two respects.
In what two respects is he praiseworthy?
He seeks wealth righteously and without violence: in this first respect he is praiseworthy.
He makes himself happy and joyful: in this second respect he is praiseworthy.
In what two respects is he blameworthy?
He seeks wealth unrighteously and by force; in this first respect he is blameworthy.
He does not share [his wealth] and does not perform meritorious deeds; in this second respect he is blameworthy.
“Headman, this enjoyer of sensual pleasures is praiseworthy for these two reasons, but censurable for these two reasons. In this regard, headman,
that enjoyer of sensual pleasures who seeks wealth both righteously and unrighteously, by violence and without violence, and having sought wealth both righteously and unrighteously,
by violence and without violence, makes himself happy and pleased, shares it, and performs meritorious deeds— [he is praiseworthy for these two reasons].”
“Headman, this enjoyer of sensual pleasures is to be praised for three reasons and criticized for one.
For which three reasons is he to be praised?
He seeks wealth righteously and without violence—this is the first reason for praise.”
"He makes himself happy and satisfied"—by this second ground he is to be praised.
"He shares [his wealth] and performs meritorious deeds"—by this third ground he is to be praised.
By what one ground is he to be censured?
"He seeks wealth unrighteously and by violence"—on account of this one ground he is to be censured.
Thus, headman, the enjoyer of sensual pleasures is praiseworthy for these three grounds and censurable for this one ground.

In that regard, headman, when a person who enjoys sensual pleasures seeks wealth righteously and without violence, yet having sought wealth righteously and without violence, does not make himself happy and pleased, nor shares it, nor performs meritorious deeds—[he is censurable on this ground].
“Headman, this enjoyer of sensual pleasures is praiseworthy in one respect and blameworthy in two respects.
In what one respect is he praiseworthy?
He seeks wealth righteously and without violence; in this one respect he is praiseworthy.”
In what two respects is he to be censured?
He does not gladden himself, nor does he satisfy himself; in this first respect he is to be censured.
He does not share [his wealth], nor does he perform meritorious deeds; in this second respect he is to be censured.
“Headman, this enjoyer of sensual pleasures is to be praised on this one ground, but censured on these two grounds. In this regard, headman,

that enjoyer of sensual pleasures who seeks wealth righteously and without violence, and having sought wealth righteously and without violence, makes himself happy and pleased, yet does not share it nor perform meritorious deeds—
this enjoyer of sensual pleasures, headman, is to be praised on two grounds and censured on one ground.”
In what two respects is he praiseworthy?
He seeks wealth righteously and without violence: in this first respect he is praiseworthy.
He makes himself happy and joyful: in this second respect he is praiseworthy.
By what one ground is he to be censured?
"He does not share [his wealth] and he does not perform meritorious deeds"—by this one ground is he to be censured.
Thus, headman, this enjoyer of sensual pleasures is praiseworthy for these two grounds and censurable for this one ground.
In this regard, headman, there is the enjoyer of sensual pleasures who seeks wealth righteously and without violence;
having sought wealth righteously and without violence, he makes himself happy and joyful, shares it, and performs meritorious deeds;
yet he enjoys that wealth while being attached to it, infatuated with it, and obsessed by it, seeing neither the danger in it nor the way of escape from it.
“Headman, this enjoyer of sensual pleasures is to be praised for three reasons and criticized for one.
For which three reasons is he to be praised?
He seeks wealth righteously and without violence—this is the first reason for praise.”
"He makes himself happy and satisfied"—by this second ground he is to be praised.
"He shares [his wealth] and performs meritorious deeds"—by this third ground he is to be praised.
By what single ground is he to be censured?

And he enjoys those riches while being obsessed with them, infatuated with them, and deeply attached to them, seeing neither their danger nor the escape from them—on account of this one ground, he is to be censured.
This enjoyer of sensual pleasures, headman, is praiseworthy on these three grounds and censurable on this one ground.

In that regard, headman, as for the enjoyer of sensual pleasures who seeks riches righteously and without violence, and having sought riches righteously and without violence, makes himself happy and pleased, shares them, and performs meritorious deeds: [he is praiseworthy].

And he enjoys those possessions without being attached to them, without being infatuated with them, without being tied to them; seeing the danger in them and possessing the wisdom of escape, he makes use of them.
This, headman, is the enjoyer of sensual pleasures who is praiseworthy for four reasons.
For what four reasons is he praiseworthy?
"He seeks wealth righteously and without violence"—by this first ground he is praiseworthy.
"He makes himself happy and joyful"—by this second ground he is praiseworthy.
"He shares [his wealth] and performs meritorious deeds"—by this third ground he is praiseworthy.

And he enjoys those possessions without being attached to them, without being infatuated by them, without being tied to them, seeing their danger and understanding the escape from them—on account of this fourth ground, he is praiseworthy.
This, headman, is the enjoyer of sensual pleasures who is praiseworthy on these four grounds.
There are, headman, these three kinds of ascetics living a life of austerity found existing in the world.
Which three?
Here, headman, a certain ascetic living a life of austerity has gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking:
“May I perhaps attain some wholesome state; may I perhaps realize a distinction in knowledge and vision that is superhuman and worthy of the noble ones.”
Thus he torments and afflicts himself, yet he does not attain wholesome states, nor does he realize any superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
But here, headman, some ascetic living a life of austerity has gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking:
"Perhaps I might attain some wholesome state; perhaps I might realize some superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones."
Thus he torments and afflicts himself, yet he does attain a wholesome state, though he does not realize the distinction of superior human states, the noble knowledge and vision.
But here, headman, some ascetic of harsh livelihood has gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, thinking:
“May I perhaps attain a wholesome state; may I perhaps realize the distinction of superior human states, the noble knowledge and vision.”
Thus he torments himself and thoroughly afflicts himself, yet he attains wholesome states and realizes a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
In this regard, headman, as for that ascetic of harsh livelihood who torments himself and thoroughly afflicts himself,
yet does not attain wholesome states nor realize a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones— [that is one case].
"Headman, this ascetic who lives a harsh life is to be censured for three reasons.
For what three reasons is he to be censured?
He torments himself and makes himself suffer—this is the first reason for censure."
"He does not attain wholesome states"—this is the second ground for censure.
"Furthermore, he does not realize any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones"—this is the third ground for censure.
This ascetic, Gāmaṇi, who lives a life of austerity, is censurable on these three grounds.

In this regard, headman, when an ascetic living a life of austerity torments and afflicts himself, even though he may attain wholesome states, he does not realize a superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
This ascetic living a life of austerity, headman, is to be criticized on two grounds and praised on one ground.
On which two grounds is he to be criticized?
"He torments himself and torments himself thoroughly"—on account of this first ground, he is to be censured.
"Furthermore, he does not realize any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones"—on account of this second ground, he is to be censured.
By what one ground is he to be praised?
"He attains wholesome states"—on account of this one ground he is to be praised.
Thus, headman, this ascetic living a life of austerity is to be censured on these two grounds and praised on this one ground.
In this regard, headman, as for that ascetic living a life of austerity who torments himself and torments himself thoroughly, yet [attains] wholesome states...
He attains it and further realizes a superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
This ascetic of austere life, O headman, is to be censured for one reason and praised for two.
For what one reason is he to be censured?
"He torments himself and torments himself thoroughly"—on account of this one ground, he is to be censured.
On account of which two grounds is he to be praised?
"He attains wholesome states"—on account of this first ground, he is to be praised.
"And he realizes a superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones"—for this second reason he is praiseworthy.
Thus, headman, this ascetic living a life of austerity is to be blamed for one reason, but praised for these two reasons.
Headman, there are these three visible fruits of the ascetic life, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be personally realized by the wise.
What are the three?
When one is lustful, on account of that lust, one intends for one’s own affliction, intends for the affliction of others, and intends for the affliction of both.
When lust has been abandoned, one does not intend for one’s own affliction, does not intend for the affliction of others, and does not intend for the affliction of both.
Weariness [of defilements] is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise.
When one is corrupted, on account of hatred, one intends for one’s own affliction, one intends for the affliction of others, and one intends for the affliction of both.
When hatred has been abandoned, one does not intend for one’s own affliction, nor does one intend for the affliction of others, nor does one intend for the affliction of both.
Weariness [of defilements] is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise.
When one is deluded, on account of that delusion, one intends for one's own affliction, one intends for the affliction of others, and one intends for the affliction of both.
When delusion has been abandoned, one no longer intends for one's own affliction, nor does one intend for the affliction of others, nor does one intend for the affliction of both.
“Wearing away [of defilements] is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise.
These, headman, are the three kinds of wearing away that are visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized by the wise.
When this was said, Rāsīya the headman said to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Bhante!
… [as before] … May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
The twelfth.

Then the householder Pāṭaliya approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: "Householder, if a noble disciple possesses four things, he is one who has reached the ultimate conclusion, one for whom there is no further state beyond this. What four? Here, householder, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. And he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are untorn, unrent, unblotched, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, not adhered to, leading to concentration. If a noble disciple possesses these four things, householder, he is one who has reached the ultimate conclusion, one for whom there is no further state beyond this. When this was said, the householder Pāṭaliya said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, in the same way the Blessed One has made the Dhamma clear in many ways. I go to the Blessed One for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may I receive the higher ordination! “Householder, one who has been a lay follower for at least ten years may receive the going forth and the higher ordination. You have been a lay follower for only a short time. Wait until you have been a lay follower for ten years, and then you may receive the going forth and the higher ordination. “Venerable sir, even if I must wait for ten years, let me receive the going forth and the higher ordination right now. Then the householder Pāṭaliya received the going forth under the Blessed One, and he received the higher ordination. And soon, not long after his higher ordination, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Pāṭaliya, by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life entered and dwelt in that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He directly knew: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. And the Venerable Pāṭaliya became one of the arahants. Then the Venerable Pāṭaliya approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him:
